screens.title: Logical vs. Physical Backups
screens.narratorSegment: In production database operations, knowing how and why your backups work can be the difference between a short recovery and catastrophic data loss. In this lesson you will learn the two primary backup families that PostgreSQL supports: logical backups, which export schema and data as S Q L or a custom archive, and physical backups, which copy the database files and WAL segments at the block level. We’ll explore their trade-offs—portability and flexibility for logical backups versus speed, comprehensiveness, and point-in-time recovery for physical backups. You’ll also see concrete tools you’ll use day-to-day: pg_dump and pg_dumpall for logical exports, and pg_basebackup plus WAL archiving for physical base backups and PITR. By the end of this chapter you’ll know which type to prefer for migrations, which to use for very large, high-transaction systems, and why most resilient plans combine both approaches. As we proceed, look for concrete examples showing when a S Q L dump is a better fit and when you must rely on WAL streaming to meet tight recovery objectives. Think about a recent change or outage you’ve faced and whether the available backups would have recovered you to the right time and state.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Logical vs. Physical Backups
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Backup strategies in PostgreSQL

Understand the practical differences and how to combine approaches for reliable disaster recovery.

Estimated lesson length: 12 minutes
In this lesson

Compare logical and physical backups, learn key tools, and plan using RPO and RTO trade-offs.

Why it matters

Choosing the wrong backup can make restores impractical or impossible under time pressure.

Chapter focus

Practical guidance: when to use pg_dump, pg_dumpall, pg_basebackup, and WAL archiving. Real examples and a hands-on activity to compare backup sizes.

Visual summary
L
Logical
SQL scripts, portable, flexible
P
Physical
Block-level copies, PITR support
Most robust plans combine both: physical for fast full recovery and PITR, logical for portability and schema-level restores.
Explore Key Topics
pg_dump — logical backup tool for single databases
pg_basebackup — physical base backup for entire cluster
WAL & PITR — reduce RPO with archived transaction logs

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to distinguish logical from physical backups, choose the right strategy based on size and recovery goals, and identify the core trade-offs each approach introduces. First, you will learn to explain what a logical backup is and how tools like pg_dump and pg_dumpall produce S Q L or custom archives that are portable across versions. Second, you will learn the characteristics of physical backups, how pg_basebackup creates consistent base images, and why WAL archiving enables point-in-time recovery. Third, you will practice mapping Recovery Point Objective and Recovery Time Objective to backup choices so you can justify a plan for a multi-terabyte cluster or a small app database. Finally, you will recognize common pitfalls — such as assuming pg_dump captures cluster-wide roles or performing an unsafe file-system copy of PGDATA while the server is running — and how to avoid them. Each objective connects to a milestone: you will evaluate a scenario and pick a backup mix, outline a PITR setup, and run a comparison exercise to observe file sizes. These skills are practical: they change how fast you can recover and how much data you can afford to lose.

Practice checklist

Use pg_dumpall for global objects
Take a pg_basebackup and verify consistency
Archive WAL files and attempt a PITR
Run a restore into a sandbox and validate roles and data
Verification tips

screens.title: Backup categories: Logical and Physical
screens.narratorSegment: Let’s define the two backup families clearly. A logical backup extracts the logical contents of the database: table definitions, rows, indexes recreated via S Q L commands, or stored in a custom archive format. Tools like pg_dump read the database and emit a script or archive that, when applied, reconstructs objects and data. The core claim is portability: because the output is S Q L or a documented archive, logical backups can often be restored to different minor or even major PostgreSQL versions, and selectively applied to individual schemas or tables. A concrete example: you can use pg_dump to export a single schema and re-import it into a development cluster, or to migrate a schema to a newer PostgreSQL instance after making small adjustments. A common misconception is that a single pg_dump captures everything in the cluster — it does not. pg_dump only handles one database; global objects like users and tablespaces require pg_dumpall. On the other hand, a physical backup copies the data directory at the file-system or block level, capturing exact binary files, configuration, and WAL segments. Physical backups are fast for very large databases and enable point-in-time recovery when paired with WAL archives. But they are tied to the server’s architecture and often the same major PostgreSQL version, so they are less portable. Consider a restore scenario: physical restores usually boot the cluster and replay WAL to a consistent state, whereas logical restores replay S Q L statements to recreate state. Each approach therefore serves different operational needs.

keyIdea.title: Fundamental difference
keyIdea.text: Logical backups export SQL-level objects and data; physical backups copy binary files and the exact cluster state including configurations and WAL.

content.html:
Definition

Logical backups

Export schema and table data as SQL scripts or a custom archive. Portable and flexible for selective restores.

Tool: pg_dump (single database)
Tool: pg_dumpall (entire instance, global objects)
Misconception
Do not assume pg_dump captures roles or tablespaces. Use pg_dumpall to capture cluster-level items.
Definition

Physical backups

Block-level copies of the PostgreSQL data directory, configuration, and WAL. Fast for large clusters and the foundation for PITR.

Tool: pg_basebackup (base backup creation)
Requires WAL archiving to enable point-in-time recovery (PITR)
Pitfall
A raw file-system copy of PGDATA while Postgres is running is not a safe backup; it will be inconsistent unless the server is shut down.
Key Takeaway

Logical for portability and selective restores; physical for speed, cluster fidelity, and PITR when paired with WAL archives.

Analogy
Think of logical backups as instructions to rebuild furniture, and physical backups as moving the assembled furniture boxes and parts intact.

screens.title: Using pg_dump and pg_dumpall
screens.narratorSegment: Now we’ll walk through the primary logical backup tools and what each captures. The tool pg_dump creates logical exports of a single database. A common command uses plain S Q L output for human-readable dumps and custom format for compressed archives suitable for pg_restore. For example, exporting a database in plain format is straightforward and yields a S Q L script you can inspect. pg_dumpall is complementary; it exports cluster-wide items such as roles and tablespaces that pg_dump skips. A frequent operational error is relying on pg_dump alone for a full instance backup, then discovering roles are missing during a restore. A concrete example: if you run pg_dump to capture a single application’s database and later restore it into a new cluster, user roles with specific permissions will not exist unless you also applied a pg_dumpall output that contains CREATE ROLE statements. Another practical point: custom-format dumps made by pg_dump can be restored more flexibly using pg_restore, which supports parallel restores for faster recovery. Finally, remember that logical backups involve reading all row data and emitting statements; for very large tables this process may be slower than a physical base backup. That trade-off is often acceptable when portability and selective restores are priority. How would you capture both data and roles for a small multi-database instance? Use pg_dump per database and run pg_dumpall for global objects.

keyIdea.title: pg_dump vs pg_dumpall
keyIdea.text: pg_dump exports a single database’s schema and data. pg_dumpall exports global cluster objects like roles and tablespaces—use both when you need a full instance restoration.

content.html:
Core Tools

pg_dump examples

Plain SQL and custom formats are common. Custom format enables parallel restore and compression.

pg_dump -U postgres -F p test_db_backup > /tmp/test_db_logical_backup.sql

pg_dump -U postgres -F c -f /tmp/test_db_logical_backup.custom test_db_backup
Plain (-F p): human-readable SQL script
Custom (-F c): compressed archive, works with pg_restore
Tip
Use custom format with parallel restore for faster restores on multi-core systems.

pg_dumpall

Capture cluster-wide roles, tablespaces, and other global objects not included by pg_dump.

pg_dumpall -U postgres > /tmp/cluster_global_objects.sql
Common mistake: skipping pg_dumpall and later finding roles missing during restore. If roles are required, include the pg_dumpall output in your recovery plan.
Key Takeaway

Use pg_dump for per-database logical backups and pg_dumpall for cluster-global items. Custom format plus pg_restore offers faster, parallel restores.

Check
After a dump, inspect the SQL or run a test restore into a sandbox to confirm roles and objects exist as expected.

screens.title: Pros and Cons of Logical Backups
screens.narratorSegment: Logical backups excel at portability and selective restoration, but they have practical limits that must guide your planning. Define the advantage first: logical backups create S Q L or custom archives, which you can apply to different servers, inspect, and selectively restore. A concrete example is migrating a development schema from production to a test cluster — pg_dump lets you grab only the required tables and import them elsewhere. However, logical backups can be slower on very large datasets because they read every row and convert it into statements or a serializable archive. During restoration they also replay S Q L, which can be time-consuming for many indexed tables or complex constraints. Another key limitation is coverage: logical backups do not capture cluster-level configuration or live transaction continuity; pg_dump does not include global roles and tablespaces unless you run pg_dumpall. A common operational mistake is relying on nightly pg_dump as the only recovery mechanism for a high-volume system with tight RPO; the restore time and potential data loss make logical-only plans risky. The right use cases for logical backups include migrations across versions, selective table restores, schema-only exports, and creating test data sets. In practice, teams often supplement logical exports with physical backups to get the best of both worlds.

keyIdea.title: Logical backups fit portability needs
keyIdea.text: Use logical backups when you need to move or inspect schema/data, but avoid them as your sole solution for large, high-transaction production clusters with tight RPO/RTO.

content.html:
Advantages
  • Portability across servers and versions when SQL is compatible.
  • Selective exports for specific tables, schemas, or data subsets.
  • Readable SQL output makes troubleshooting and partial restores easier.
Example: Export a schema to replicate into a test environment for feature testing or debugging.
Limitations
  • Slower for very large databases during backup and restore.
  • Does not capture cluster-wide global objects unless pg_dumpall is used.
  • Restores replay SQL which may be slower than file-level restore for big datasets.
Misconception: pg_dump equals full-instance backup. Verify global objects separately.
When to use logical backups
Small-to-medium databases where portability, migrations, or selective restores dominate. Combine with physical backups for full disaster recovery.

screens.title: Physical Backups and pg_basebackup
screens.narratorSegment: Physical backups operate at the file-system level, copying PostgreSQL’s data directory so that the restored cluster has the exact set of files and configuration present at the time of the backup. The primary tool for creating a consistent physical base backup of a running cluster is pg_basebackup. It coordinates with the server to ensure files are consistent and can include an option to stream WAL during the backup process. The practical benefit is speed: copying blocks is usually faster than exporting and replaying S Q L for very large datasets. Physical backups also capture global objects and configuration files automatically because you are copying the entire PGDATA tree. Crucially, physical backups become the foundation for Point-in-Time Recovery when you also archive WAL files continuously. In a PITR setup you restore a base backup and then replay archived WAL segments to move the database forward to a specific transaction point. A common confusion is thinking you can simply copy PGDATA while the server runs; without coordination that produces inconsistent and likely corrupted backups. pg_basebackup handles this coordination. Another operational detail: physical backups are less portable across major versions and architecture differences, so they are best used for like-for-like restores and disaster recovery on compatible systems. Your backup plan should include periodic base backups and correct WAL archiving for coverage between bases.

keyIdea.title: Why physical backups matter
keyIdea.text: Physical backups capture the exact cluster files and configuration and, with WAL, enable precise point-in-time recovery — essential for low RPO environments.

content.html:
What it copies
  • All on-disk data files for tables and indexes
  • Configuration files present in PGDATA
  • WAL segments when archived or streamed
Benefit: Fast backup and restore for very large datasets; suitable as disaster-recovery foundation.
Tool: pg_basebackup

pg_basebackup coordinates with the server to produce a consistent base backup and supports streaming WAL for coverage during the backup.

pg_basebackup -U postgres -D /tmp/test_db_physical_backup -F tar -X stream -P
Remember: a file-system copy of PGDATA without coordination is unsafe if the server is running.
Key Takeaway

Use pg_basebackup for fast, consistent base backups. Combine base backups with archived WAL files to achieve point-in-time recovery.

screens.title: WAL Archiving and Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)
screens.narratorSegment: Write-Ahead Logs, or WAL, are the transaction logs that record every change to the database files. For robust recovery, you pair a physical base backup with a continuous stream of archived WAL files. The concept is simple: the base backup gives you a starting point, and each archived WAL file contains the sequence of changes that occurred after that base. To perform a point-in-time recovery, you restore the base backup and then replay archive WAL files until you reach the desired transaction moment. A practical example: if an accidental DELETE occurred at 14:32, and you have WALs archived continuously, you can restore the base backup and replay WALs up to 14:31:59 to recover to the state just before the delete. Setting this up requires configuring archive_mode and an archive_command to copy WAL files to a durable storage location. A common mistake is failing to archive WALs reliably or losing archive ranges; without the needed WAL segments you cannot reach the desired transaction point. Another operational note: WAL retention and storage planning matter — continuous archiving increases storage needs, and you must plan retention and cleanup carefully. Finally, test your PITR by performing a restore to a sandbox and replaying WALs to the chosen point in time so you know the process and timing under pressure.

keyIdea.title: WAL enables precise recovery
keyIdea.text: Archived WAL segments let you advance a physical base backup forward to a specific transaction point, enabling point-in-time recovery and very low logical data loss.

content.html:
Process

PITR sequence

1. Take a consistent physical base backup (pg_basebackup)
2. Configure archive_mode and archive_command to copy WAL files to durable storage
3. On restore, restore base backup then replay archived WALs until the desired time
4. Test the restore into a sandbox and validate application-level data

Practical notes

  • WAL archiving increases storage needs — plan retention and lifecycle.
  • Missing WAL files mean you cannot reach the intended recovery point.
  • Simulate accidental deletes and test recovery to confirm procedures work.
Key Takeaway

PITR requires both a consistent base backup and reliable WAL archiving; do not assume either alone provides full recovery capabilities.

screens.title: Choosing a Strategy: RPO & RTO
screens.narratorSegment: Recovery Point Objective and Recovery Time Objective are the business constraints that translate directly into technical backup choices. RPO defines the maximum acceptable data loss — how stale the recovered data can be. RTO defines the maximum acceptable downtime — how long the system can be unavailable. For example, if the business requires an RPO measured in minutes and an RTO measured in minutes, logical nightly dumps will not suffice. Instead you prioritize physical base backups plus continuous WAL archiving so you can replay transactions up to the most recent archived WAL. Conversely, if you support several small, independent applications where portability and schema migration are key and downtime is tolerable, logical backups via pg_dump and scheduled restores for testing may be preferable. A common misjudgment is treating RPO and RTO as independent of backup size; in practice, large databases increase restore times and storage requirements, so you must measure how long a restore actually takes. A practical decision path: map desired RPO to WAL archive frequency and base backup cadence, and map desired RTO to restore automation and parallelism. Always run timed restore drills to validate your RTO assumptions. When in doubt, combine approaches: physical backups plus WAL for disaster recovery and periodic logical dumps for migrations and easy selective restores.

keyIdea.title: RPO & RTO guide choices
keyIdea.text: Low RPO requires frequent WAL archiving and physical backups; low RTO demands fast restore procedures and automation. Map business constraints to technical actions and test them.

content.html:
Decision factors
Low RPO & RTO → physical backups + WAL archiving + restore automation
Portability & migration → logical backups with pg_dump and pg_dumpall
Large data sets → physical backups are faster to create and restore
Run a restore drill, measure time-to-restore, and incorporate those timings into your RTO commitments. Remember that storage and network speed constrain both backup and restore operations.
Example scenarios
  • Several small apps needing migration: choose logical backups for portability.
  • Multi-terabyte, high-traffic cluster needing minute-level RPO: prioritize physical backups with WAL.
Key Takeaway

Translate business RPO/RTO into backup cadence and automation. Validate assumptions with timed restore drills and monitoring of archive completeness.

screens.title: Activity: Comparing Backup File Sizes
screens.narratorSegment: This activity walks you through creating a test database, populating it, and taking both logical and physical backups so you can compare file sizes and contents. Start by creating a test database and a table populated with, for example, 100,000 rows to represent a realistic dataset. Then run pg_dump in plain and custom formats to produce two logical backups. Next, ensure archive_mode is off for a simple comparison, and run pg_basebackup to create a physical backup of the entire cluster data directory. Finally, use standard tools to compare the resulting file sizes. The point of this exercise is to see that logical backups may be smaller or larger depending on data types and compression, while physical backups copy the full data directory. The hands-on example also reveals what each backup actually includes: logical backups contain DDL and INSERT statements or compressed archives of tuples, while physical backups include configuration and internal files. A good verification step is to restore the logical dump into a sandbox and check row counts, then extract the physical backup and attempt to start a copy of the cluster to confirm consistency. Doing these steps will make the differences concrete and help you choose which backup type serves your operational goals.

keyIdea.title: Observe differences firsthand
keyIdea.text: Create a sample dataset, run pg_dump and pg_basebackup, then compare sizes and contents to understand what each backup stores and restores.

content.html:
Setup
CREATE DATABASE test_db_backup;

CREATE TABLE large_table (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(100),
  description TEXT,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- Insert 100,000 rows (example using generate_series)
INSERT INTO large_table (name, description)
SELECT
  'Item ' || generate_series,
  md5(random()::text) || md5(random()::text) || md5(random()::text)
FROM generate_series(1, 100000);
Commands
pg_dump -U postgres -F p test_db_backup > /tmp/test_db_logical_backup.sql
pg_dump -U postgres -F c -f /tmp/test_db_logical_backup.custom test_db_backup

pg_basebackup -U postgres -D /tmp/test_db_physical_backup -F tar -X stream -P

# Compare sizes
du -sh /tmp/test_db_logical_backup.sql /tmp/test_db_logical_backup.custom /tmp/test_db_physical_backup
Reflection
Record the sizes and note what each backup contains. Restore the logical dump to confirm schema and row counts. For the physical backup, extract and verify the PGDATA layout. These checks confirm both content and consistency.

screens.title: Designing a Multi-Layered Backup Plan
screens.narratorSegment: A resilient backup plan typically layers multiple backup types to satisfy both disaster recovery and operational needs. The baseline is periodic physical base backups scheduled according to recovery requirements; these are fast to create and restore for large datasets. Layer on continuous WAL archiving so you can fill gaps between base backups and achieve point-in-time recovery. Then add regular logical dumps for portability, schema snapshots, and easy selective restores. An example schedule could be weekly physical base backups, continuous WAL archiving, and nightly logical dumps of critical databases for migration and testing. Important design choices include storage location for archives, retention policies for WAL files and base backups, and automation for both backup creation and test restores. A frequent operational mistake is not validating retention: old WAL files consumed by retention policies might be removed before you verify they are safely backed up elsewhere. Make automation robust: monitor archive successes, alert on failed uploads, and periodically run restore drills. Finally, document recovery steps clearly so that during an incident your team can follow the tested procedure without improvisation. The layered approach gives you fast recovery paths and the flexibility to migrate or inspect data when needed.

keyIdea.title: Layered approach
keyIdea.text: Combine periodic physical base backups with WAL archiving and supplementary logical dumps to meet both recovery and operational needs.

content.html:
Plan elements
  1. Scheduled physical base backups (e.g., weekly)
  2. Continuous WAL archiving with monitored uploads
  3. Nightly logical dumps for portability and testing
  4. Retention policies and periodic cleanup of old backups
  5. Automated restore drills and monitoring with alerts
Operational tips
  • Store backups and WAL archives off primary storage to survive hardware failures.
  • Validate every backup with a restore into a sandbox on a regular cadence.
  • Automate alerts for archive_command failures to prevent silent data gaps.
Key Takeaway

A layered backup plan balances speed, portability, and durability. Automate, monitor, and test restores to ensure the plan meets RPO and RTO commitments.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Teams often make avoidable mistakes when implementing backups. One frequent error is assuming pg_dump alone captures cluster-wide state; roles and tablespaces are omitted unless pg_dumpall is run. Another is performing a file-system copy of PGDATA while Postgres is running; this leads to inconsistent and corrupted backups unless the server is stopped. Silent failures in WAL archiving are another hazard — if archive_command fails and alerts are not configured, WAL segments will be missing, and PITR will be impossible for those time ranges. Storage planning mistakes include underestimating archived WAL storage and retention needs, which can cause automatic deletion of segments you later need. Testing is the most underused safeguard: a backup that hasn’t been restored in a sandbox hasn’t been proven. A practical avoidance plan includes always automating and monitoring archive_command, scheduling regular restore drills, including pg_dumpall outputs when cluster-level recovery capability is needed, and documenting the full recovery process. These steps reduce surprises and ensure that when an incident happens, your recovery is reliable and repeatable. Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them means do not rely on untested backups, unmonitored wal archiving, or unsafe file copies. automate, monitor, and validate restores regularly.. In practical terms, operational traps that cause backups to fail or be incomplete. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoid operational traps
keyIdea.text: Do not rely on untested backups, unmonitored WAL archiving, or unsafe file copies. Automate, monitor, and validate restores regularly.

content.html:
Common mistakes
  • Using pg_dump alone for full-instance recovery without pg_dumpall.
  • Copying PGDATA while the server is running (unsafe and inconsistent).
  • Not monitoring archive_command failures and losing WAL segments silently.
  • Failing to test restores periodically.
How to avoid
  1. Include pg_dumpall when cluster-level objects matter.
  2. Use pg_basebackup for physical backups instead of ad-hoc file copies.
  3. Monitor archive_command and set alerting for failures.
  4. Schedule and document restore drills to validate your backups.
Pro Tip

Treat backup validation as part of your release and maintenance checklist. A successful backup that can’t be restored is not a backup.

screens.title: Restore Drills and Validation
screens.narratorSegment: Validation is the final and most important step in any backup strategy. A restore drill shows whether your backups, WAL archives, and procedures actually succeed under realistic conditions. A practical drill includes restoring a logical dump into a sandbox and confirming schema and row counts, restoring a physical base backup and replaying WALs to a known point in time, and verifying user roles and permissions when pg_dumpall was used. When you run these drills, time the entire operation to validate RTO assumptions and record any manual steps that could be automated. Also check for missing WAL segments, permission errors, or restored configuration mismatches. If any step fails, update your backup procedures and automation and repeat the drill until it succeeds reliably. A common misconception is that a successful backup file transfer proves recoverability; it does not. Only a completed restore demonstrates that the backup contains the information and structure your application requires. Make these drills part of change control and maintenance windows so they are performed regularly and tracked. keyIdea.title: Validate with restores
keyIdea.text: Regular restore drills confirm data, roles, WAL completeness, and timing. Time your restores to ensure RTO goals are achievable.

content.html:
Validation Checklist
  1. Restore a logical dump to a sandbox, verify schema and row counts.
  2. Restore a physical base backup, replay WALs to a chosen point, and confirm data integrity.
  3. Apply pg_dumpall output to restore roles and tablespaces, and check permissions.
  4. Time each step and log the total duration to validate RTO.
  5. Document issues and remediate, then rerun the drill until it succeeds reliably.
What to record
  • Start and finish times for each restore step
  • Any missing WAL segments or permission errors
  • Manual steps that could be automated
Key Takeaway

Only a successful restore proves recoverability. Schedule and document restore drills, and use their timing to validate your RTO commitments.

Quick definitions
Logical Backup

fullNarratorScript:
In production database operations, knowing how and why your backups work can be the difference between a short recovery and catastrophic data loss. In this lesson you will learn the two primary backup families that PostgreSQL supports: logical backups, which export schema and data as S Q L or a custom archive, and physical backups, which copy the database files and WAL segments at the block level. We’ll explore their trade-offs—portability and flexibility for logical backups versus speed, comprehensiveness, and point-in-time recovery for physical backups. You’ll also see concrete tools you’ll use day-to-day: pg_dump and pg_dumpall for logical exports, and pg_basebackup plus WAL archiving for physical base backups and PITR. By the end of this chapter you’ll know which type to prefer for migrations, which to use for very large, high-transaction systems, and why most resilient plans combine both approaches. As we proceed, look for concrete examples showing when a S Q L dump is a better fit and when you must rely on WAL streaming to meet tight recovery objectives. Think about a recent change or outage you’ve faced and whether the available backups would have recovered you to the right time and state.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to distinguish logical from physical backups, choose the right strategy based on size and recovery goals, and identify the core trade-offs each approach introduces. First, you will learn to explain what a logical backup is and how tools like pg_dump and pg_dumpall produce S Q L or custom archives that are portable across versions. Second, you will learn the characteristics of physical backups, how pg_basebackup creates consistent base images, and why WAL archiving enables point-in-time recovery. Third, you will practice mapping Recovery Point Objective and Recovery Time Objective to backup choices so you can justify a plan for a multi-terabyte cluster or a small app database. Finally, you will recognize common pitfalls — such as assuming pg_dump captures cluster-wide roles or performing an unsafe file-system copy of PGDATA while the server is running — and how to avoid them. Each objective connects to a milestone: you will evaluate a scenario and pick a backup mix, outline a PITR setup, and run a comparison exercise to observe file sizes. These skills are practical: they change how fast you can recover and how much data you can afford to lose.

This second objectives slide focuses on hands-on and judgment skills you will practice. You will run and interpret pg_dump outputs, learn when pg_dumpall is required to capture cluster-wide roles and tablespaces, and perform a pg_basebackup to understand how physical snapshots behave. You will compare output sizes from logical and physical backups to see what each contains and why file sizes differ. Importantly, you will practice one key operational skill: testing a restore. The chapter emphasizes that an untested backup is hazardous; running restores into a sandbox environment confirms that global objects and WAL archives were captured correctly. Finally, you will practice scenario-based decisions: for a small app database pick a logical-only plan for portability; for a multi-terabyte, high-transaction cluster, design a physical base backup schedule with continuous WAL archiving for PITR. Each skill is paired with a verification step so you can demonstrate competency and reason about trade-offs in real deployments.

Let’s define the two backup families clearly. A logical backup extracts the logical contents of the database: table definitions, rows, indexes recreated via S Q L commands, or stored in a custom archive format. Tools like pg_dump read the database and emit a script or archive that, when applied, reconstructs objects and data. The core claim is portability: because the output is S Q L or a documented archive, logical backups can often be restored to different minor or even major PostgreSQL versions, and selectively applied to individual schemas or tables. A concrete example: you can use pg_dump to export a single schema and re-import it into a development cluster, or to migrate a schema to a newer PostgreSQL instance after making small adjustments. A common misconception is that a single pg_dump captures everything in the cluster — it does not. pg_dump only handles one database; global objects like users and tablespaces require pg_dumpall. On the other hand, a physical backup copies the data directory at the file-system or block level, capturing exact binary files, configuration, and WAL segments. Physical backups are fast for very large databases and enable point-in-time recovery when paired with WAL archives. But they are tied to the server’s architecture and often the same major PostgreSQL version, so they are less portable. Consider a restore scenario: physical restores usually boot the cluster and replay WAL to a consistent state, whereas logical restores replay S Q L statements to recreate state. Each approach therefore serves different operational needs.

Now we’ll walk through the primary logical backup tools and what each captures. The tool pg_dump creates logical exports of a single database. A common command uses plain S Q L output for human-readable dumps and custom format for compressed archives suitable for pg_restore. For example, exporting a database in plain format is straightforward and yields a S Q L script you can inspect. pg_dumpall is complementary; it exports cluster-wide items such as roles and tablespaces that pg_dump skips. A frequent operational error is relying on pg_dump alone for a full instance backup, then discovering roles are missing during a restore. A concrete example: if you run pg_dump to capture a single application’s database and later restore it into a new cluster, user roles with specific permissions will not exist unless you also applied a pg_dumpall output that contains CREATE ROLE statements. Another practical point: custom-format dumps made by pg_dump can be restored more flexibly using pg_restore, which supports parallel restores for faster recovery. Finally, remember that logical backups involve reading all row data and emitting statements; for very large tables this process may be slower than a physical base backup. That trade-off is often acceptable when portability and selective restores are priority. How would you capture both data and roles for a small multi-database instance? Use pg_dump per database and run pg_dumpall for global objects.

Logical backups excel at portability and selective restoration, but they have practical limits that must guide your planning. Define the advantage first: logical backups create S Q L or custom archives, which you can apply to different servers, inspect, and selectively restore. A concrete example is migrating a development schema from production to a test cluster — pg_dump lets you grab only the required tables and import them elsewhere. However, logical backups can be slower on very large datasets because they read every row and convert it into statements or a serializable archive. During restoration they also replay S Q L, which can be time-consuming for many indexed tables or complex constraints. Another key limitation is coverage: logical backups do not capture cluster-level configuration or live transaction continuity; pg_dump does not include global roles and tablespaces unless you run pg_dumpall. A common operational mistake is relying on nightly pg_dump as the only recovery mechanism for a high-volume system with tight RPO; the restore time and potential data loss make logical-only plans risky. The right use cases for logical backups include migrations across versions, selective table restores, schema-only exports, and creating test data sets. In practice, teams often supplement logical exports with physical backups to get the best of both worlds.

Physical backups operate at the file-system level, copying PostgreSQL’s data directory so that the restored cluster has the exact set of files and configuration present at the time of the backup. The primary tool for creating a consistent physical base backup of a running cluster is pg_basebackup. It coordinates with the server to ensure files are consistent and can include an option to stream WAL during the backup process. The practical benefit is speed: copying blocks is usually faster than exporting and replaying S Q L for very large datasets. Physical backups also capture global objects and configuration files automatically because you are copying the entire PGDATA tree. Crucially, physical backups become the foundation for Point-in-Time Recovery when you also archive WAL files continuously. In a PITR setup you restore a base backup and then replay archived WAL segments to move the database forward to a specific transaction point. A common confusion is thinking you can simply copy PGDATA while the server runs; without coordination that produces inconsistent and likely corrupted backups. pg_basebackup handles this coordination. Another operational detail: physical backups are less portable across major versions and architecture differences, so they are best used for like-for-like restores and disaster recovery on compatible systems. Your backup plan should include periodic base backups and correct WAL archiving for coverage between bases.

Write-Ahead Logs, or WAL, are the transaction logs that record every change to the database files. For robust recovery, you pair a physical base backup with a continuous stream of archived WAL files. The concept is simple: the base backup gives you a starting point, and each archived WAL file contains the sequence of changes that occurred after that base. To perform a point-in-time recovery, you restore the base backup and then replay archive WAL files until you reach the desired transaction moment. A practical example: if an accidental DELETE occurred at 14:32, and you have WALs archived continuously, you can restore the base backup and replay WALs up to 14:31:59 to recover to the state just before the delete. Setting this up requires configuring archive_mode and an archive_command to copy WAL files to a durable storage location. A common mistake is failing to archive WALs reliably or losing archive ranges; without the needed WAL segments you cannot reach the desired transaction point. Another operational note: WAL retention and storage planning matter — continuous archiving increases storage needs, and you must plan retention and cleanup carefully. Finally, test your PITR by performing a restore to a sandbox and replaying WALs to the chosen point in time so you know the process and timing under pressure.

Recovery Point Objective and Recovery Time Objective are the business constraints that translate directly into technical backup choices. RPO defines the maximum acceptable data loss — how stale the recovered data can be. RTO defines the maximum acceptable downtime — how long the system can be unavailable. For example, if the business requires an RPO measured in minutes and an RTO measured in minutes, logical nightly dumps will not suffice. Instead you prioritize physical base backups plus continuous WAL archiving so you can replay transactions up to the most recent archived WAL. Conversely, if you support several small, independent applications where portability and schema migration are key and downtime is tolerable, logical backups via pg_dump and scheduled restores for testing may be preferable. A common misjudgment is treating RPO and RTO as independent of backup size; in practice, large databases increase restore times and storage requirements, so you must measure how long a restore actually takes. A practical decision path: map desired RPO to WAL archive frequency and base backup cadence, and map desired RTO to restore automation and parallelism. Always run timed restore drills to validate your RTO assumptions. When in doubt, combine approaches: physical backups plus WAL for disaster recovery and periodic logical dumps for migrations and easy selective restores.

The baseline is periodic physical base backups scheduled according to recovery requirements; these are fast to create and restore for large datasets. Layer on continuous WAL archiving so you can fill gaps between base backups and achieve point-in-time recovery. Then add regular logical dumps for portability, schema snapshots, and easy selective restores. An example schedule could be weekly physical base backups, continuous WAL archiving, and nightly logical dumps of critical databases for migration and testing. Important design choices include storage location for archives, retention policies for WAL files and base backups, and automation for both backup creation and test restores. A frequent operational mistake is not validating retention: old WAL files consumed by retention policies might be removed before you verify they are safely backed up elsewhere. Make automation robust: monitor archive successes, alert on failed uploads, and periodically run restore drills. Finally, document recovery steps clearly so that during an incident your team can follow the tested procedure without improvisation. The layered approach gives you fast recovery paths and the flexibility to migrate or inspect data when needed.

Teams often make avoidable mistakes when implementing backups. One frequent error is assuming pg_dump alone captures cluster-wide state; roles and tablespaces are omitted unless pg_dumpall is run. Another is performing a file-system copy of PGDATA while Postgres is running; this leads to inconsistent and corrupted backups unless the server is stopped. Silent failures in WAL archiving are another hazard — if archive_command fails and alerts are not configured, WAL segments will be missing, and PITR will be impossible for those time ranges. Storage planning mistakes include underestimating archived WAL storage and retention needs, which can cause automatic deletion of segments you later need. Testing is the most underused safeguard: a backup that hasn’t been restored in a sandbox hasn’t been proven. A practical avoidance plan includes always automating and monitoring archive_command, scheduling regular restore drills, including pg_dumpall outputs when cluster-level recovery capability is needed, and documenting the full recovery process. These steps reduce surprises and ensure that when an incident happens, your recovery is reliable and repeatable. Validation is the final and most important step in any backup strategy. A restore drill shows whether your backups, WAL archives, and procedures actually succeed under realistic conditions. A practical drill includes restoring a logical dump into a sandbox and confirming schema and row counts, restoring a physical base backup and replaying WALs to a known point in time, and verifying user roles and permissions when pg_dumpall was used. When you run these drills, time the entire operation to validate RTO assumptions and record any manual steps that could be automated. Also check for missing WAL segments, permission errors, or restored configuration mismatches. If any step fails, update your backup procedures and automation and repeat the drill until it succeeds reliably. A common misconception is that a successful backup file transfer proves recoverability; it does not. Only a completed restore demonstrates that the backup contains the information and structure your application requires. Make these drills part of change control and maintenance windows so they are performed regularly and tracked. These three concise points capture what you should remember going forward. First, logical backups export S Q L or custom archives offering portability and selective restores — ideal for migrations and test data preparation. Second, physical backups copy the data directory and, when combined with WAL archiving, enable fast restores and precise point-in-time recovery for low RPO environments. Third, backup planning must be driven by RPO and RTO, and every plan requires regular restore tests. A final practical reminder: include pg_dumpall when cluster-wide objects are necessary, and never rely on an untested file-system copy for an online cluster. Keep these ideas in mind as you design and run backup procedures so that your backups become reliable instruments for recovery, not a source of false confidence. Keep these brief definitions handy when making backup decisions. Logical Backup: export of schema and data as S Q L or a custom archive, best for portability and selective restores. Physical Backup: block-level copy of PGDATA and related files, used for fast restores and as the foundation for PITR when WALs are archived. Point-in-Time Recovery: restoring a base backup and replaying archived WAL segments to reach a specified transaction moment. Use these terms to describe your backup plan succinctly to colleagues and stakeholders and to document the recovery steps in incident runbooks.
